title: The Comprehensive to the Container Port: k-punk, the Unit, and the Lost Future
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Leicestershire, the Comprehensive and the Terrace

stops.name: Leicester: a birth in the East Midlands
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'). No hospital or street address is established in any source consulted; the coordinate is Leicester city centre.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of July a son is born in Leicester to a working-class household: the father an engineering technician, the mother a cleaner, both of them conservative in politics and unremarkable in the census of an industrial county. No hospital is named in any record that can be read. The family lives a dozen miles north at Loughborough, and the boy grows up inside the ordinary English arrangement of shift work, a comprehensive school, and a music press that talks to teenagers as though they were adults. They call him Mark.
suggested_refs: Leicester civil registration district, birth of 11 July 1968

stops.name: Loughborough: the comprehensive and the music press
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Wikipedia attests that he grew up in Loughborough to working-class, conservative parents and attended a local comprehensive; the school is not named in any consulted source and the date is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: He goes to the local comprehensive, whose name no source records. What educates him is bought weekly at a newsagent: the New Musical Express in its imperial years, post-punk records reviewed by writers who assume a sixteen-year-old can be addressed in the language of theory. The argument he will conduct about class for the next forty years starts in the house he is living in, where the parents are conservative and the son is not. Football holds the other half of his attention. The club is Nottingham Forest.
suggested_refs: The New Musical Express of the late 1970s and early 1980s, the post-punk critical apparatus Fisher credits as his first education

stops.name: University of Hull: English and Philosophy
stops.date_confidence: the BA in English and Philosophy taken at Hull in 1989 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'); the 1986 matriculation is inferred from a standard three-year degree and is not attested.
stops.campa: Fisher reads English and Philosophy at Hull, on the flat estuary edge of the East Riding, and takes his degree in 1989. It is the last stretch of British higher education still funded as though it were owed to him: a grant, a hall, a library, no debt at the end of it. Here the philosophy syllabus and the record collection are set to argue with each other, and neither is treated as the illustration of the other. He will spend much of his working life describing what replaced the grant.
suggested_refs: The University of Hull English and Philosophy degree of 1989

stops.name: Hillsborough Stadium, Sheffield: the semi-final
stops.date_confidence: attested that Fisher was present at the Hillsborough disaster (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'). Date, fixture, stand allocation and the toll of 97 are attested separately (Wikipedia, 'Hillsborough disaster'). The undergraduate framing and friends' accounts of the disaster's lasting political effect on him are [R], dossier-only.
stops.campa: Liverpool against Nottingham Forest, FA Cup semi-final. The Forest supporters are put in the South Stand and the Spion Kop; the Liverpool end is Leppings Lane, where the crush begins and where ninety-seven people are finally counted dead. Fisher is in the ground. What follows across the next quarter century, the police accounts, the newspaper front page, the decades of official denial and the slow forcing of the truth, is a working demonstration of how a state describes working-class people to themselves. He is twenty years old.
suggested_refs: The Hillsborough Independent Panel report (2012) and the second inquests (2016)

segments.name: Warwick and the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit

stops.name: University of Warwick: the postgraduate arrives
stops.date_confidence: [R] on the date: Wikipedia attests only that Fisher completed a PhD at Warwick in 1999, so the arrival year is an ordering device. Supervision by Sadie Plant is unverified and is not asserted here: no fetched source states it. The coordinate is the campus pin already fixed in the corpus for Warwick, not the county town, which lies some ten kilometres south.
stops.campa: Fisher comes to Warwick for postgraduate work in philosophy and finds a department where the reading list has gone strange. Cybernetics, jungle twelve-inches, science fiction and continental theory are handled as though they were engineering manuals for the same machine. He is in his early twenties, and for the first time his two educations, the seminar and the record shop, are one subject. The campus is not in the county town of Warwick at all: concrete blocks standing in fields outside Coventry, on the Kenilworth road.
suggested_refs: The University of Warwick philosophy department of the early 1990s
sources: nick_land.journey.json, campus pin 52.38 / -1.56167 and its note distinguishing campus from county town

stops.name: University of Warwick: D-Generation and Entropy in the UK
stops.date_confidence: the 1994 twelve-inch Entropy in the UK on Mythago is attested (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'), as are the second EP Concrete Island and the later Isle Of The Dead as The Lower Depths. The stop is plotted at Fisher's Warwick pin because no source places him in Manchester: Simon Reynolds calls D-Generation 'this Manchester trio', which describes the band, not Fisher's residence, and a Manchester pin for him would be unsupported.
stops.campa: Fisher makes records. The trio is called D-Generation, the twelve-inch is Entropy in the UK, the label is Mythago, the year is 1994, and the music is breakbeat hardcore made by people who have read too much and are not sorry about it. A second EP takes the title Concrete Island. The project continues afterwards as The Lower Depths, which releases Isle Of The Dead. Almost nobody hears any of it. In 2021 a collector recovers the tapes and a small label presses Entropy in the UK again, artwork intact, twenty-seven years late.
suggested_refs: D-Generation, Entropy in the UK (Mythago, 1994), reissued by Kokoxoka Records as KR019 on 4 February 2021
Simon Reynolds, 'D-Generation, or the Dawn of K-Punk', reynoldsretro.blogspot.com, November 2018
sources: Kokoxoka Records Bandcamp page for Entropy in the UK

stops.name: University of Warwick: the unit is formalized
stops.date_confidence: attested with a fuzzy edge (Wikipedia, 'Cybernetic Culture Research Unit'): Sadie Plant formed the collective around 1993-94 and the unit was formalized at Warwick in late 1995. Fisher is named a founding member in Wikipedia's article on him. A single founding year overstates what the sources give.
stops.campa: Sadie Plant has been gathering the collective since 1993 or 1994. In the last weeks of 1995 it acquires a name, the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit, and a room to be thrown out of later. Fisher is a founding member. The method is to treat theory as a species of fiction and fiction as an intelligence report: numbers, demons, sound systems, a future arriving early and from underneath. For a few years the seminar and the rave are held to be one institution, and nobody in the room thinks this is a figure of speech. Nick Land becomes the driving force once Plant goes.
suggested_refs: CCRU, Abstract Culture swarm pamphlets, Warwick, 1996-1998

stops.name: University of Warwick: Sadie Plant leaves
stops.date_confidence: attested that Plant left her Warwick post and that Land became the unit's driving force after her departure (Wikipedia, 'Cybernetic Culture Research Unit'); the roster of figures passing through the milieu is taken from nick_land.journey.json, stop 1997-01-01, which names Fisher among them.
stops.campa: Plant resigns her Warwick post, and the unit loses the cyberfeminist who assembled it. What is left gathers around Nick Land and gets stranger and less institutional by the term. Kodwo Eshun passes through the room in these years, and Ray Brassier, Reza Negarestani and Steve Goodman; Fisher is already in it, a postgraduate some years into a thesis. The Abstract Culture pamphlets go out under the unit's name. The university, for its part, has never fully conceded that the unit exists at all.
suggested_refs: Robin Mackay, 'Nick Land: An Experiment in Inhumanism' (2012), on the unit after Plant

stops.name: University of Warwick: Flatline Constructs
stops.date_confidence: attested that Fisher completed the doctorate at Warwick in 1999 with the thesis Flatline Constructs: Gothic Materialism and Cybernetic Theory-Fiction (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'). No fetched source gives a month, so the July date that circulates is not used. Land's 1998 resignation and the seminar's move to a Leamington Spa flat are attested on his own file; no source names Fisher at either event.
stops.campa: The thesis is called Flatline Constructs: Gothic Materialism and Cybernetic Theory-Fiction. It argues that cybernetics and the Gothic are the same argument told twice over, that the machine and the ghost are one device seen from two sides, and it submits this to an examinations office as a doctorate in philosophy. Nick Land has resigned his lectureship the year before and the seminar has moved into a flat in Leamington Spa with no institutional address at all. Fisher writes the unit's case in the format the institution accepts. It passes.
stops.quote: Humans are only an impediment to the full Realization of Capital as machinic-fecund death.
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher, Flatline Constructs (Warwick doctoral thesis, 1999; reissued by Exmilitary Press, 2018)

stops.name: Orpington College, Kent: philosophy in further education
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the Orpington College post, and the surrounding period of precarious temporary work and depression, come from the dossier's summary of Fisher's own autobiographical essays and were not confirmed in any fetched source. No start or end date is established anywhere consulted; the year orders the segment.
stops.campa: The doctorate leads nowhere an academic career would recognize. Fisher takes hours teaching philosophy, religious studies and critical thinking at a further-education college in Orpington, at the outer edge of London where Kent begins, marking coursework for students who are in the room because the labour market has told them to be. The years are precarious, badly paid and mostly undocumented, and the depression that will later occupy his writing is at its worst inside them. He publishes nothing. What is known about this period is mostly what he says about it afterwards.
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher's autobiographical essays on the post-doctoral years, collected in k-punk (Repeater, 2018)
sources: Dossier, /home/drdoeg/taller/Colegio_Invisible/working/journeys/dossiers/mark_fisher.dossier.md, unverified in a fetched source

stops.name: London: the k-punk blog begins
stops.date_confidence: attested that the blog was launched in 2003 (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'). No source ties the launch to an address, so the coordinate is a general London placeholder rather than a located place.
stops.campa: He starts a blog and calls it k-punk. The form has no editor, no word count, no commissioning process and no money in it, and that is precisely its use: he can write. Films, hardcore continuum records, television, depression, the class politics of a call centre, each at whatever length the thought takes and posted the night it is finished. Within a couple of years the blog is being read by people who will spend the next decade arguing with it. He says later that the informality let him trick himself back into working.
suggested_refs: k-punk.abstractdynamics.org and k-punk.org, the blog archive 2003-2016

stops.name: London: Dissensus
stops.date_confidence: the co-founding of the message board Dissensus with Matt Ingram is attested (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'). The 2004 date appears in no fetched source and is [R]. Wikipedia does not attach the pseudonym Woebot to Ingram, though the dossier does.
stops.campa: With the writer Matt Ingram he sets up a message board called Dissensus. It is a forum in the old sense: threads that run for years, arguments conducted at length by people using handles, a small population of critics, producers and obsessives working out in public what the last twenty years of British music had been for. Much of what later appears as chapters is first put up here and taken apart by strangers, unkindly and in detail. The blog is where he thinks aloud; this is where he is contradicted.
stops.quote: Part of the problem with online debate culture is that it operates on the implicit principle that there is an infinite time to rehearse and nuance positions.
stops.quote_source: Mark Fisher, 'Capitalist Realism after the crash', k-punk, 13 December 2009
suggested_refs: The Dissensus board archive, 2004 onward
sources: k-punk.org, 'Capitalist Realism after the crash', 13 December 2009 (fetched directly)

stops.name: London: londonunderlondon, with Justin Barton
stops.date_confidence: attested by The Showroom's own Mark Fisher page: he produced two audio-essays in collaboration with Justin Barton, londonunderlondon (2005) and On Vanishing Land (2013). No venue or address is given for the 2005 work, so the coordinate is a general London placeholder.
stops.campa: Fisher and Justin Barton make an audio essay about London from underneath: sewers, rivers put into pipes, tunnels, the buried city the surface city stands on and does not mention. They walk the ground, they record it, and the argument arrives as sound rather than as a paragraph. Voice, field recording and music are cut together into something that is neither a lecture nor a radio documentary and has no obvious shelf to sit on. It is the first of two such works the pair will make. The second comes eight years later.
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher and Justin Barton, londonunderlondon (2005)
sources: The Showroom, 'Mark Fisher' relationship page, theshowroom.org (fetched directly)

stops.name: Port of Felixstowe: the walk begins
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the 2006 walk and its Felixstowe starting point are dossier-only. The Showroom's Mark Fisher page confirms the Barton collaboration and dates On Vanishing Land to 2013, but says nothing about a 2006 walk or where it started. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Two men set out on foot from the largest container port in Britain. Gantry cranes work the ships in a line along the water, boxes coming off Asia at a rate nobody standing on the quay can follow; behind them the Suffolk coast runs north into marsh, shingle and low fields. Fisher and Barton are walking in order to look at exactly this, the machinery of world trade set down beside a landscape older than writing. Nothing is being filmed and nothing is being staged. What survives of the walk is what the two of them assemble seven years later.
suggested_refs: The Port of Felixstowe container terminals, starting point of the Suffolk coast walk
sources: Dossier, mark_fisher.dossier.md, unverified in a fetched source
The Showroom, 'Mark Fisher' relationship page (for the Barton collaboration itself)

stops.name: Sutton Hoo, Suffolk: the ship under the mounds
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the walk's endpoint is dossier-only, consistent with a Felixstowe-to-Suffolk-coast route but not independently verified in any fetched source. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The walk ends near the burial mounds above the river Deben, where an Anglo-Saxon ship was hauled up the hill and buried with a king inside it, and where the timbers rotted away over thirteen centuries leaving only the stain of themselves in the sand. Fisher is working towards a word for what a landscape does when it holds something the people standing in it cannot account for. The eerie is not the same as the horrible. It is a presence where there should be absence, or an absence where there should be a presence.
stops.quote: Themes of incursion, by unnameable forces, geological sentience or temporal anomaly, recur throughout
stops.quote_source: Mark Fisher, 'On Vanishing Land', k-punk, 15 January 2013
suggested_refs: The Sutton Hoo ship burial and its sand-stain, National Trust, Suffolk
sources: Dossier, mark_fisher.dossier.md, unverified in a fetched source

segments.name: The Wire, and a Book Everyone Quotes

stops.name: The Netherlands: Underground Resistance
stops.date_confidence: attested by The Wire's own obituary: Fisher began writing for the magazine in 2007 and his first cover feature was an interview with Underground Resistance conducted in the Netherlands that year. No city is named in the source, so the coordinate is Amsterdam standing in for the country. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The Wire sends him to meet Underground Resistance, the Detroit techno collective that gives no faces and few interviews, and he comes back with his first cover feature. The subject suits him exactly: a group who treat dance records as communiqués from a war, who refuse the photograph, and who insist a label can be a political organization rather than a distribution arrangement. He has been writing for nothing on a blog for four years. He is now being paid to do it, at length, on the front of a magazine.
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher's Underground Resistance cover feature, The Wire, 2007

stops.name: Corbet Place, Spitalfields: acting deputy editor
stops.date_confidence: attested that Fisher became acting deputy editor of The Wire in 2008 and served roughly a year (The Wire, 'Mark Fisher 1968-2017'). The obituary names no address; the coordinate is the magazine's editorial base of that period, 23 Jack's Place, Corbet Place, London E1. A commonly circulated coordinate near Tower Bridge Road matches no address the magazine has used and is not adopted here.
stops.campa: For about a year he holds a desk job: acting deputy editor of The Wire, in offices off Brick Lane. He had come to the magazine the year before as a contributor and is now on the other side of the commissioning. He edits, subs copy, argues about covers, and writes on Tricky, Mark Stewart, Ultra-red and Burial. It is the nearest he ever comes to a conventional career inside the trade he is best at. It lasts twelve months. Then he goes back to teaching hours and freelance rates.
suggested_refs: The Wire, issues of 2007-2009, Fisher's contributions on Burial, Tricky, Mark Stewart and Ultra-red
sources: thewire.co.uk/contact (for the magazine's addresses of record)

stops.name: New Alresford, Hampshire: The Resistible Demise of Michael Jackson
stops.date_confidence: attested that Fisher edited the multi-author collection The Resistible Demise of Michael Jackson for Zero Books in 2009 (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'); the month is an ordering device and is not attested. The coordinate is John Hunt Publishing's Hampshire address of record for the imprint, not a place Fisher is known to have worked.
stops.campa: Jackson dies in June and Fisher has a book about it assembled before the year is out: two dozen writers on a body rebuilt in public, on Motown as a factory floor, on the child star as an industrial product with a shelf life and a legal team. He edits rather than writes it, which is the other thing he is good at, gathering people who would not otherwise appear between the same covers and setting them a deadline short enough to be interesting. The imprint he has just helped start is a few months old, and the first use he puts it to is convening other people. The book is out before the end of 2009.
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher (ed.), The Resistible Demise of Michael Jackson (Zero Books, 2009)

stops.name: New Alresford, Hampshire: Zero Books and Capitalist Realism
stops.date_confidence: attested that Zero Books was established in 2009 by Tariq Goddard and Mark Fisher as an imprint of John Hunt Publishing (Wikipedia, 'Zero Books'), and that Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative? was published by Zero in 2009 (Wikipedia, 'Capitalist Realism'). The month orders the segment. The book's most quoted sentence is not reproduced here as a quotation: no fetched source showed it in the body text, and Fisher himself credits the formulation to Fredric Jameson and Slavoj Zizek.
stops.campa: A short book, published by an imprint he has helped found inside a small Hampshire publisher better known for mind-body-spirit titles. The argument is that capitalism has stopped being a system that can be argued with and has become the weather: the outer limit of what anyone is able to picture, so complete that it no longer needs defending. For the first chapter he takes up a formulation he credits to Fredric Jameson and to Slavoj Zizek, that it is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism. The phrase gets away from him entirely.
stops.quote: Everything is impossible now, including the so-called status quo.
stops.quote_source: Title of Matthew Fuller's Mute interview with Mark Fisher, linked from k-punk, 25 December 2009
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher, Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative? (Zero Books, 2009)
slavoj_zizek.journey.json, stop 1989-12-01, Meard Street: The Sublime Object of Ideology

stops.name: London: k-punk after the crash
stops.date_confidence: attested: the post 'Capitalist Realism after the crash' is dated 13 December 2009 and 'Post-Apocalypse Now' 29 November 2009, both fetched directly at k-punk.org.
stops.campa: The banks have been rescued and nothing else has changed, and the blog keeps working at what that means at post length rather than book length. In the same weeks he writes about eco-apocalypse as the one future capitalist realism is content to put on a screen, because a dead planet is cheaper to show than a different economy. He is careful in these posts about what is his and what is borrowed. A postal worker's blog and a paragraph of Fredric Jameson are quoted at length and under their own names, rather than absorbed into his voice.
stops.quote: The standard tactic of capitalist realism in relation to eco-apocalypse is to work with the stupid ingenuity of the Symbolic.
suggested_refs: Roy Mayall, 'Not Nostalgia', London Review of Books blog, 3 December 2009, quoted by Fisher
Fredric Jameson, Valences of the Dialectic (2009), quoted by Fisher on k-punk, 25 December 2009
sources: k-punk.org, 'Capitalist Realism after the crash', 13 December 2009 (fetched directly)

segments.name: Hours, and a Shirt from Coney Island

stops.name: City Lit, Covent Garden: hours in adult education
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the City Lit teaching is dossier-only and was not confirmed in any fetched source. No complete appointment chronology for Fisher's teaching years was found anywhere consulted, and the date orders the segment rather than fixing an event.
stops.campa: Between the blog and the books there is the actual job, and the job is hours. He teaches at City Lit, the adult education institute a street away from the opera house, to rooms of people who have come after work to be taught philosophy by a man with a doctorate and no permanent post. A book of his about why nothing can be otherwise is selling steadily in the shops on the same street. The institute is publicly funded, unglamorous, does the thing universities advertise, and is being cut year on year. He is paid by the hour.
suggested_refs: City Lit, Keeley Street, Covent Garden, the adult education institute
sources: Dossier, mark_fisher.dossier.md, unverified in a fetched source

stops.name: University of East London, Docklands: another set of hours
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the University of East London post is dossier-only and appears in no fetched source; Wikipedia does not mention the university in connection with Fisher at all. The coordinate is the Docklands campus on Woolwich Manor Way, E16, resolved from OpenStreetMap; a coordinate near Canning Town that circulates for this stop is about 2.9 km wrong. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Fisher teaches here too, on an hourly rate, on short contracts, with a long commute at either end of the day. The students are among the first cohorts to be charged properly for a degree, and the man taking them through the reading has published a book about why that arrangement presents itself as the only conceivable one. He does the work and goes home on the DLR. The campus stands along the north side of the Royal Albert Dock: purpose-built student towers put up on water that used to load ships.
suggested_refs: University of East London, Docklands Campus, Woolwich Manor Way, E16
sources: Dossier, mark_fisher.dossier.md, unverified in a fetched source

stops.name: Coney Island, Brooklyn: a shirt for his son
stops.date_confidence: attested in Michael Schapira's interview with Fisher, Full Stop, published 8 December 2011: on his first trip to New York City he made a point of finding time to head out to Coney Island and pick up a Warriors shirt for his young child. The interview fixes the trip as no later than December 2011; no exact date for the visit is given. A frequently circulated 2013 URL for this interview returns 404; the 2011 one resolves.
stops.campa: First time in New York, and the errand he makes time for is the subway to the end of the line. The Warriors ends at Coney Island: a gang walks the length of the city through one night to get back to a boardwalk in the cold, and that walk is the film. He buys a Warriors shirt for his son. He mentions it to an interviewer that December, among questions about capitalism and the university, as the thing he had made a point of finding time for. It is winter and the boardwalk is out of season.
suggested_refs: Michael Schapira, interview with Mark Fisher, Full Stop, 8 December 2011

stops.name: London: why mental health is a political issue
stops.date_confidence: [R] on the date and the venue: the essay 'Why Mental Health Is a Political Issue' is reported in the dossier as published in The Guardian on 16 July 2012, and the Guardian site was not fetchable in this pass, so neither the date nor the placement is independently confirmed. The coordinate is a general London placeholder.
stops.campa: He puts the argument in a national newspaper: that the epidemic of depression and anxiety in Britain is not a problem of individual brain chemistry to be met one prescription at a time, but a political fact with a history, produced by insecure work, debt, and thirty years of instruction that a person's circumstances are their own doing. He is writing it from inside the condition he is describing, which is where the tone of the piece comes from. The claim is unremarkable now. It was not in 2012.
stops.quote: Collective depression is the result of the ruling class project of resubordination.
stops.quote_source: Mark Fisher, 'Good for Nothing', The Occupied Times, 19 March 2014
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher, 'Why Mental Health Is a Political Issue', The Guardian, reported as 16 July 2012
sources: Dossier, mark_fisher.dossier.md; The Guardian not fetchable in this pass
theoccupiedtimes.org, 'Good For Nothing', 19 March 2014 (fetched directly), for the quotation

stops.name: The Showroom, Penfold Street: On Vanishing Land
stops.date_confidence: attested by The Showroom: Mark Fisher and Justin Barton presented On Vanishing Land there from 6 February to 6 April 2013, at 63 Penfold Street. The claim that this was its first public presentation is not on the cited page and is not made here; the same page records a December 2019 event, 'Incursions, Departures', as presenting the two audio-essays together for the first time.
stops.campa: Seven years after the walk, the Suffolk coast is installed in a gallery off the Edgware Road and left running for two months: voice, field recording and music, played into a room that a listener sits down in. Container cranes, a buried ship, a marsh, the same shoreline crossed on foot in 2006 and reassembled out of tape. The piece is not about Suffolk. It is about what a landscape does to the people crossing it, and the word the two of them keep returning to for that is the eerie.
stops.quote: the contemporary cultural fascination with the illogics of the Eerie
stops.quote_source: Mark Fisher, 'On Vanishing Land', k-punk, 15 January 2013
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher and Justin Barton, On Vanishing Land, The Showroom, 63 Penfold Street, 6 February to 6 April 2013
sources: The Showroom, 'Mark Fisher' relationship page, theshowroom.org (fetched directly)

stops.name: London: Exiting the Vampire Castle
stops.date_confidence: attested: published 24 November 2013, first at The North Star and republished at openDemocracy, fetched directly. The coordinate is a general London placeholder; the essay has no place attached to it.
stops.campa: He writes an essay attacking what the online left does to its own: the reflex of the call-out, the competitive policing of language, the conversion of politics into a machine for establishing which speaker is least guilty. He names the apparatus the Vampire Castle and argues that it works by turning class into a matter of individual sin and then feeding on the result. The reaction is immediate and very large, some of it proving his point and some of it not. He never retracts the piece and never writes another like it.
stops.quote: The personal is political because there is no personal. There is no private realm to retreat into.
stops.quote_source: Mark Fisher, 'Remember Who The Enemy Is', k-punk, 25 November 2013
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher, 'Exiting the Vampire Castle', The North Star and openDemocracy, 24 November 2013
sources: k-punk.org, 'Remember Who The Enemy Is', 25 November 2013 (fetched directly)

stops.name: Goldsmiths, New Cross: the Department of Visual Cultures
stops.date_confidence: attested that Fisher was a lecturer in Goldsmiths' Department of Visual Cultures, course leader for the MA Contemporary Art Theory and before that for the MA in Aural and Visual Cultures (Goldsmiths tribute page); Wikipedia calls him a visiting fellow and lecturer in Aural and Visual Cultures. No source gives a start date, so the 2013 pin is an ordering device and the 2013-2017 range that circulates is unsupported.
stops.campa: Goldsmiths takes him. New Cross, south-east London, a department that studies images and sound as objects in their own right rather than as illustrations of something else, and a job with a title attached to a salary. He leads the MA in Aural and Visual Cultures and afterwards the MA in Contemporary Art Theory. Students apply to the college because he is at it. After a decade and a half of hours and short contracts he has, in his mid-forties, a proper academic post, and it will run for about three and a half years.
suggested_refs: Goldsmiths, University of London, Department of Visual Cultures
sources: Goldsmiths, 'Mark Fisher' tribute page, gold.ac.uk/news/mark-fisher/ (fetched directly)

stops.name: New Alresford, Hampshire: Ghosts of My Life
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ghosts of My Life: Writings on Depression, Hauntology and Lost Futures was published by Zero Books in 2014 (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'); the month is an ordering device. Derrida's coinage of hantologie in Spectres de Marx (1993) is attested (Wikipedia, 'Hauntology'), which also records that Simon Reynolds and Fisher applied the term to music in the 2000s; it does not present either usage as derived from the other, and no such derivation is claimed here.
stops.campa: The second book gathers a decade of the blog into a single argument about time: that popular culture after the millennium stopped producing the future it had produced every few years since the war and began reissuing itself instead. The depression and the cultural argument are handled as a single argument, which is what makes the book difficult to shelve. He takes the name for it from Jacques Derrida, who coined hantologie in Spectres de Marx in 1993 for a present haunted by a future that never arrived. Fisher carries the word out of philosophy and into record reviews.
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher, Ghosts of My Life (Zero Books, 2014)
jacques_derrida.journey.json, Paris pin, for Spectres de Marx (1993)

stops.name: London: Good for Nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested: published in The Occupied Times on 19 March 2014, fetched directly at theoccupiedtimes.org. The coordinate is a general London placeholder for the paper produced out of the Occupy camps.
stops.campa: He writes about his own depression as an argument rather than as a confession. The point is not that he suffered. The point is that the shape his suffering took, the flat certainty of being worthless, was manufactured, and taught to a working-class boy by an education system that had an exact use for the lesson. Magical voluntarism is his name for the doctrine that everyone is the author of their own condition, and he puts his own case in as evidence against it. The piece runs in The Occupied Times, a free paper produced out of the Occupy camps, in March 2014.
stops.quote: My depression was always tied up with the conviction that I was literally good for nothing.
stops.quote_source: Mark Fisher, 'Good for Nothing', The Occupied Times, 19 March 2014

stops.name: Cecil Court, London: Repeater Books
stops.date_confidence: attested by Repeater's own about page: Repeater Books was founded in 2014 by Mark Fisher, Tariq Goddard, Etan Ilfeld, Phil Jourdan, Matteo Mandarini, Alex Niven and Tamar Shlaim. The commonly circulated founder list omitting Ilfeld and Jourdan is wrong and is corrected here. The month orders the segment. The coordinate is Watkins Media's Cecil Court address, a publisher placeholder rather than the site of any documented Fisher event.
stops.campa: The relationship with the parent company breaks and the editors walk out together. Fisher leaves with Tariq Goddard, Etan Ilfeld, Phil Jourdan, Matteo Mandarini, Alex Niven and Tamar Shlaim, and they start again as Repeater Books, backed by Watkins Media out of a booksellers' alley off Charing Cross Road. The premise is unchanged from Zero: short, cheap, argumentative books by writers the trade will not commission, published quickly. Everything he publishes from here on comes out under this imprint, including the volumes assembled after his death.

stops.name: Brighton: the pier and the Burger King
stops.date_confidence: attested in Craig Gent, 'Mark Fisher, 1968-2017', Novara Media, 19 January 2017, which places the Brighton talk in March 2015 and describes taking in the pier and the sea before taking refuge in the Burger King on the seafront. The day is not given. A frequently cited /01/14/ URL for this obituary returns 404; the 19 January one resolves.
stops.campa: He comes down to Brighton in March to give a talk. Afterwards there is the pier and the sea in the cold, and then the two of them take refuge in the Burger King on the seafront, because in March that is what is open. The man is being read across the English-speaking left and he is indoors on the seafront at Brighton, out of the wind, talking. Craig Gent writes it down two years later because it is the sort of thing a person keeps: not the talk, the burger place.

stops.name: Ipswich: the local meeting
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the dossier reports Fisher supporting anti-austerity organizing in Ipswich, as part of an engagement running through the student protests, Occupy and the People's Assembly. None of this was confirmed in a fetched source and the date is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: Suffolk is not a county with a left in it. He lives on the coast and does the ordinary work anyway: the local anti-austerity meeting, the room above a pub, the twenty people who turn up on a weeknight. The student occupations of 2010 and the Occupy camps had persuaded him that the horizon he had described in print could be moved after all, and the years afterwards go into keeping a small piece of that alive in a county town. No record survives of what was said at any of these meetings.

Argentina has been conducting its own long argument about whether there is an alternative, in a currency that keeps collapsing under the people holding it, and the book arrives in the middle of that argument rather than at the start of one. The phrase realismo capitalista enters Spanish-language criticism and stays there. Fisher never goes to Buenos Aires.

stops.name: New Cross Gate station: the overland ride
stops.date_confidence: [R] and undated in the source: Craig Gent's Novara Media obituary describes a single occasion on which Fisher suggested they head to New Cross Gate station together and talked on the short overland ride back into London. It is one remembered afternoon and not a documented Felixstowe-to-Goldsmiths commuting routine, as it is sometimes rendered. The 2016 date orders the segment. Coordinate resolved from OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: After the seminar he suggests they walk down to the station together rather than say goodbye at the college gate. Ten minutes along New Cross Road past the shops, then the overland train north into London, and a conversation for the length of the ride. Craig Gent sets it down six days after the death, because it is what he has to set down: not a position, not an argument, an ordinary walk to the train with a man who was easy to talk to on the way. What they said on the train he does not report.

stops.name: Goldsmiths, New Cross: Postcapitalist Desire
stops.date_confidence: the seminar's existence is attested: Goldsmiths' tribute page states that Fisher taught the MA special subject Vocalities and Postcapitalist Desire. stops.campa: The last course he teaches puts a question the left has largely refused to ask: what do people actually want, and can anything be built out of wanting that is not simply the shopping. He works through Marcuse, Lukacs, Lyotard, Nancy Hartsock, and Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari, in a seminar room, with a recorder running because a student is recording it. Four years later those recordings are published as a book, carrying his name and the student's editing. The course does not finish.
stops.quote: Capital has insinuated itself everywhere, into our pleasures and our dreams as much as our work.

stops.name: King Street, Felixstowe: the last year begins
stops.date_confidence: attested via the inquest-era reporting summarized in Wikipedia that Fisher's mental health markedly worsened from May 2016. The King Street address is attested (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)'); the coordinate is resolved from OpenStreetMap, and a seafront coordinate about 1.4 km southeast that circulates for this address is not used.
stops.campa: The house is on King Street in Felixstowe, a town of a pier, a container port and a long shingle beach. From May his mental health gets markedly worse. He is teaching in London two hours up the line, finishing a book, running an imprint, and writing about depression as a political condition while living inside one. What is on record about that summer in the house comes from an inquest held afterwards rather than from a biographer, and it is thin. It establishes the direction and almost nothing else.

stops.name: Cecil Court, London: The Weird and the Eerie
stops.date_confidence: attested that The Weird and the Eerie, Fisher's final sole-authored book, was published by Repeater Books around the turn of 2016-17; Wikipedia gives 2017. No exact publication date was confirmed in this pass, and the month used here orders the segment. The coordinate is Repeater's publisher address of record.
stops.campa: The last book he writes alone takes two words usually filed under horror and pulls them apart. The weird is what does not belong and is here regardless. The eerie is the cry of a bird over an empty marsh: a landscape with an agency in it that cannot be located, or a silence where a voice ought to be. The examples come from fiction, film and records rather than from philosophy. It is the least directly political thing he publishes. He is writing it on a shingle coast with a container port at one end of it and a marsh at the other.

stops.name: Ipswich Hospital, Heath Road: December
stops.date_confidence: attested via Wikipedia's inquest-era account that Fisher was admitted to Ipswich Hospital in December 2016 after a suspected overdose; no day is given. stops.campa: He is admitted after a suspected overdose and treated on Heath Road, inland from the house and the beach. A few weeks earlier he had published a book about landscapes with something wrong in them that nobody standing there is able to point to. The family goes looking for psychiatric care beyond the admission itself. What survives of that search is an account given afterwards at an inquest, and what it describes is a service that had been reorganized and a referral back into it. Then it is December, and he is at home, and the record of the next fortnight is empty.
stops.quote: The dominant school of thought in psychiatry locates the origins of such 'beliefs' in malfunctioning brain chemistry.

stops.name: King Street, Felixstowe: the telephone appointments
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, citing inquest reporting): Fisher sought psychiatric treatment in the weeks leading up to his death, but his general practitioner had only been able to offer meetings over the phone. This is frequently misreported as a psychiatric service offering telephone consultations; it was the GP. Only the month is fixed.
stops.campa: In the weeks before he dies he asks for help, and what is available to him is a telephone. Not a psychiatric service, and this is the detail most often got wrong afterwards: it is his own general practitioner, who can offer meetings over the phone and not in a room. He has argued in print for most of a decade that the treatment of mental illness in Britain was privatized into a question of individual brain chemistry. He was in a hospital bed in December. It is January now, the house is on King Street, and the appointments are calls.

stops.name: King Street, Felixstowe: 13 January 2017
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Mark Fisher (writer)', and The Wire's obituary): Fisher died by suicide at his home on King Street, Felixstowe, on 13 January 2017, aged 48. The clause that a coroner recorded a conclusion of suicide, which circulates attached to this account, appears in no fetched source and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: He dies at home, by his own hand, on the thirteenth of January. He is forty-eight. He leaves a wife, Zoe, and a son; a lecture course with sessions still to run; an imprint he founded two years earlier; and a body of writing that had argued for most of a decade that the misery he was inside had been manufactured rather than earned. The Wire, where he had once sat as deputy editor, prints an obituary that records no funeral, no burial and no memorial, and ends on the two dates: 11 July 1968 to 13 January 2017.

No plaque, no bust and no named room appears in any account that can be read. What the college institutes instead is an annual lecture, first held in 2018.
